tier_reason: Chapter03/02_branch.C holds BM_branched and BM_branchless but no results; the 3.5x figure exists only in the book (first-party, Clang 11, no flags or CPU model). The published BM_branchless does not perform the task: `a[b1[i]] += p1[i]` on `unsigned long* a[2]` advances the stored pointers instead of adding to a1/a2, so the timed loop is not equivalent to the baseline and is undefined behaviour, leaving no valid measurement behind the claim.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Book only (not in the repository): the pointer-array branchless loop about 3.5 times faster than the if/else loop with an unpredictable condition. The repository's BM_branchless that this figure refers to does not compute the sums (see caveats), so the ratio is not a same-task comparison.
corrections.caveats: [verify] Harness defect: in Chapter03/02_branch.C, BM_branchless declares `unsigned long* a[2] = { &a2, &a1 };` and times `a[b1[i]] += p1[i];`, which adds p1[i] to the pointer stored in a[] (pointer arithmetic) instead of to the accumulator it points at (that would need `*a[b1[i]] += p1[i]`). a1 and a2 stay 0, the pointers are moved far outside their objects (undefined behaviour, so the compiler may transform the loop arbitrarily), nothing checks the result, and the loop is not equivalent to BM_branched. BM_branchless2a has the same bug. The record's own workload text ("a[b1[i]] += p1[i] with a two-pointer array") suggests the book prints the same code, so the 3.5x ratio cannot be tied to a correct implementation. The value-array variants in the same file (BM_branched1 against BM_branchless1, BM_branched2 against BM_branchless2) are correct same-task comparisons, but no numbers for them are claimed here. All BENCHMARK registrations are commented out and the benchmark argument is 1<<22 elements (ARGS macro).

notes: Downgraded to D for a no-valid-measurement harness defect (pointer arithmetic instead of accumulation, UB) rather than rejected, since the book's measurement may or may not have used this exact code; orchestrator may treat it like the stb-zip different-result precedent. corrections.caveats: [verify] Checked the two order books by diff: they differ only in the two map members (std::array<std::array<MEOrder*, 1M>, 256> and std::array<MEOrdersAtPrice*, 256> against nested std::unordered_map and std::unordered_map<Price, ...>), the array variant using bounds-checked .at() and the unordered_map variant using operator[] (which inserts default entries on cancel lookups of unknown orders) plus one extra find() in getOrdersAtPrice. tier_reason: The Arm Community post (Nov 2013, Arm intern, first-party) could not be opened (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND developer.arm.com); search snippets confirm it benchmarks CMSIS-DSP FFTs against a Numerical Recipes radix-2 float FFT and an adapted Roberts/Slaney/Bouras fixed-point FFT on a Cortex-M4 with zero-wait-state memory, but the speedup figures are snippet-only and no benchmark code, flags or committed results are public, so at most C.

corrections.caveats: [verify] The verifier's own searches confirmed the post's setup (CMSIS-DSP FFT against the Numerical Recipes radix-2 float FFT and a 32-bit adaptation of the Roberts/Slaney/Bouras fixed-point FFT, Cortex-M4, zero-wait-state memory, FPU enabled) but did not surface the 35x, 4x or 1.9x figures, so those remain unconfirmed search-summary numbers. Likely mechanism for the large float gap (inference, not stated in any opened source): the Numerical Recipes four1 routine keeps its twiddle recurrence in double, which a single-precision-only Cortex-M4F FPU must emulate in software, so the baseline is handicapped on this core. Further counter-evidence opened: SYLT-FFT's README (Freescale Kinetis K20 Cortex-M4, Keil 5.01 -O3 and GCC 4.8.4 -O3) reports its 256-point fixed-point inverse FFT 25.6% (Keil) and 15.1% (GCC) faster than arm_cfft_radix2_q31 from CMSIS-DSP 1.4.2, so tuned plain-C FFTs can beat the library's radix-2 Q31 path.
